steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on tight bounds for learning homotopy type from samples, in the style of Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger, for subsets of Euclidean space and Riemannian manifolds. Motivate topological inference from point samples, recall the Niyogi-Smale-Weinberger result, and explain how we generalize it and what we prove.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivating question: inferring topology from partial geometric information
2. Origins in shape reconstruction; later relevance to learning and TDA
3. The Niyogi-Smale-Weinberger result and its consequences
4. Our generalizations: ambient space, types of sets
5. Main results: conditions on sample density/noise, interval of radii, tightness

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivating question
- can we infer the topology of a set from partial geometric information? under which conditions?

2. Origins and later relevance
- first motivated by shape reconstruction of objects in 3-dimensional Euclidean space
- partial information = finite, generally noisy, point set from photogrammetric or lidar measurements
- more recently: learning and topological data analysis (TDA)
- recover (relatively) low-dimensional support of a probability measure in high-dimensional space from (finite) data drawn from it
- support assumed a manifold -> manifold learning

3. Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger
- C^{2} manifold of positive reach in Euclidean space + sufficiently dense sample on (or near) it
- union of balls of certain radii centred on sample captures homotopy type
- nerve theorem: same homotopy type for Čech complex and \alpha -complex of the sample
- from these complexes: learn topological information, e.g. homology groups
- numerous generalizations

4. Our generalizations
- revisit Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger, generalize settings in various ways
- ambient space: Euclidean space \mathbb{R}^{d} and Riemannian manifolds with bounded sectional curvature; new version of reach in Riemannian setting inspired by cut locus (Definition 13)
- sets: sets of positive reach and manifolds of positive reach
- sets of positive reach need not be manifolds, can have varying dimensions (Figure 1)
- manifolds with positive reach are C^{1,1} smooth (differentiable, Lipschitz derivative); significantly larger family than C^{2} manifolds with positive reach

5. Main results
- set (or manifold) {\mathcal{S}} of positive reach, sample P
- two sample quality parameters: density \varepsilon, noisiness \delta; encoded via one-sided Hausdorff distances between P and {\mathcal{S}}
- explicit conditions on \varepsilon, \delta: exists r s.t. union of balls of radius r centred at P deformation-retracts to {\mathcal{S}}
- NSW only considered \delta=0 and \delta=\varepsilon; tight bounds only in latter case (Figure 2)
- interval of radii r (equation (4)) -> guarantee of successful homotopy inference
- tightness: specific {\mathcal{S}} and P (Propositions 8, 9, 47, and 48) where homotopy not inferrable if conditions fail

The first motivation for these questions was the shape reconstruction of objects in 3-dimensional Euclidean space. In that setting the partial geometric information was a finite set of points, in general noisy, obtained from photogrammetric or lidar measurements.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Can the topology of a set be inferred if we only have partial geometric information about it? And under which conditions can this inference be done?

The first motivation for these questions was the shape reconstruction of objects in 3-dimensional Euclidean space. In that setting the partial geometric information was a finite set of points, in general noisy, obtained from photogrammetric or lidar measurements.

More recently the same questions have come up in learning and in topological data analysis (TDA). There one wants to recover a (relatively) low-dimensional support of a probability measure in a high-dimensional space, given a (finite) data set that is drawn from this probability measure. If the support is assumed to be a manifold, this process is called manifold learning.

In prior work, Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger showed that if we have a C^{2} manifold of positive reach embedded in Euclidean space and a point sample on (or near) the manifold that is dense enough, then the union of balls of certain radii centred on the point sample captures the homotopy type of the manifold. By the nerve theorem, the Čech complex and \alpha -complex of the point sample have the same homotopy type as the union of balls. From these complexes we can then learn topological information like the homology groups of the underlying manifold. The homotopy learning result of Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger has led to many generalizations.

In this article we revisit the work of Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger and generalize their settings in several ways.

The first generalization is about the ambient space. We consider both the Euclidean space \mathbb{R}^{d} and Riemannian manifolds with bounded sectional curvature. For this we introduce a new version of the reach in the Riemannian setting, which is inspired by the cut locus (see Definition 13).

The second generalization is about the types of sets we study. We consider sets of positive reach and manifolds of positive reach. Sets of positive reach don't have to be manifolds, in fact they can have varying dimensions (see for example Figure 1). Manifolds with positive reach are C^{1,1} smooth, which means they are differentiable with Lipschitz derivative. This is a much larger family of sets than the C^{2} manifolds with positive reach that Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger considered.

Like in the work of Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger, our setting is a set (or a manifold) {\mathcal{S}} of positive reach and a sample P of it. We have two sample quality parameters, the sample density \varepsilon and the sample noisiness \delta, and we encode them using one-sided Hausdorff distances between P and {\mathcal{S}}. We give explicit conditions on \varepsilon and \delta under which there is a parameter r such that the union of balls of radius r centred at the sample P deformation-retracts to {\mathcal{S}}. This expands on the work of Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger, who only considered the cases \delta=0 and \delta=\varepsilon, and who only got tight bounds in the latter case (see Figure 2).

Also, given a set of positive reach {\mathcal{S}} and a sample P of it, we identify an interval of radii r (equation (4)) for which the union of balls of radius r centred at P deformation-retracts to {\mathcal{S}}. So we give a guarantee that the homotopy inference of {\mathcal{S}} from P is successful. We also show that for a specific choice of {\mathcal{S}} and P (see Propositions 8, 9, 47, and 48), the homotopy of {\mathcal{S}} cannot be inferred from P if our conditions on \varepsilon and \delta do not hold, which proves that our bounds are tight in terms of \varepsilon and \delta.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Can we infer the topology of a set if we are only given partial geometric information about it? Under which conditions is such inference possible?

These questions were first motivated by the shape reconstruction of objects in 3-dimensional Euclidean space. There, the partial geometric information was given by a finite, in general noisy, set of points obtained from photogrammetric or lidar measurements [1,2,3,4,5].

More recently, the same questions have arisen in learning and topological data analysis (TDA). In these fields, one wants to recover a (relatively) low-dimensional support of a probability measure in a high-dimensional space, given a (finite) data set drawn from this probability measure [6,7,8,9]. When the support is assumed to be a manifold, this process is called manifold learning [10].

In [11], Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger showed that, given a C^{2} manifold of positive reach embedded in Euclidean space and a sufficiently dense point sample on (or near) the manifold, the union of balls of certain radii centred on the point sample captures the homotopy type of the manifold. By the nerve theorem [8], the Čech complex [12,13] and \alpha -complex [14] of the point sample share the homotopy type of the union of balls. From these complexes we can then learn topological information such as the homology groups of the underlying manifold. The homotopy learning result of Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger has led to numerous generalizations including [15,16,17,18,19].

In this article, we revisit the work of Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger, generalizing their settings in various ways.

The first generalization concerns the ambient space — we consider both the Euclidean space \mathbb{R}^{d} and Riemannian manifolds with bounded sectional curvature. To this end, we introduce a new version of the reach in the Riemannian setting, inspired by the cut locus (see Definition 13).

The second generalization lies in the types of sets we study — we consider sets of positive reach and manifolds of positive reach. Sets of positive reach need not be manifolds — in fact, they can have varying dimensions (see for example Figure 1). Manifolds with positive reach are C^{1,1} smooth, i.e., differentiable with Lipschitz derivative. This is a significantly larger family of sets than the C^{2} manifolds with positive reach considered by Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger.

As in the work of Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger, our setting consists of a set (or a manifold) {\mathcal{S}} of positive reach and its sample P. We distinguish two sample quality parameters — sample density \varepsilon and sample noisiness \delta, which we encode using one-sided Hausdorff distances between P and {\mathcal{S}}. We give explicit conditions on \varepsilon and \delta under which there exists a parameter r such that the union of balls of radius r centred at the sample P deformation-retracts to {\mathcal{S}}. Furthermore, given a set of positive reach {\mathcal{S}} and its sample P, we identify an interval of radii r (equation (4)) for which the union of balls of radius r centred at the sample P deformation-retracts to {\mathcal{S}}. We thus provide a guarantee for successful homotopy inference of {\mathcal{S}} from the sample P. Moreover, we show that for a specific choice of {\mathcal{S}} and P (see Propositions 8, 9, 47, and 48), the homotopy of {\mathcal{S}} cannot be inferred from P if our conditions on \varepsilon and \delta are not satisfied, which proves that our bounds are tight in terms of \varepsilon and \delta.
